Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
Each of the four Vedas—the basic scriptures of Hinduism—has been divided into four sections, of which the ब्राह्मणस् form the second. They are in prose and generally deal with the practical aspects of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa is the only extant ब्राह्मण of the Atharvaveda. Unlike the other ब्राह्मणस् of the other three वेदस् (for e.g., the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa) this work is considered as not so ancient. It is later than 2000 B. C., but earlier than 1000 B. C.
Generally the sūtra literature of the वेदाङ्गस् like the श्रौतसूत्रस्, follow the ब्राह्मणस्. But here, this ब्राह्मण, in its latter part, appears to follow the Vaitānasūtras (the श्रौतसूत्रस् of the Atharvaveda).
This ब्राह्मण is in two parts: The Pūrva-Gopatha and the Uttara-Gopatha. The former has five prapāṭhakas (chapters) and a total of 135 kaṇḍikās (short sections). The latter has six prapāṭhakas and 123 kaṇḍikās. Each kaṇḍikā contains five or six long sentences.
According to one view, this ब्राह्मण might have been composed at a time when the Atharvaveda was officially admitted into the group of the वेदस् which were only three for a long time. (See ATHARVA-VEDA.) Its language is not archaic nor is there a well-knit order in the presentation of the ideas. Many words and phrases from the उपनिषद्स् as also ākhyānakas (stories) find a place here. However, its style in general resembles that of the other ब्राह्मणस्.
The text starts with a description of च्रेअतिओन् from ब्रह्मन् which alone existed in the beginning. This च्रेअतिओन् started with water and then, through it, the sages like भृगु, अथर्वन् and the ten Ātharvaṇa sages evolved. Further च्रेअतिओन् proceeded from them in this order. the Atharvaveda, प्रणव (Oṅkāra), the three worlds, अग्नि, वायु and सूर्य, the three वेदस्, Oceans, वरुण (the presiding deity of the oceans and the water principle), the sage Āṅgirasa and his descendants, the five quarters (the four directions and the sky above), the subsidiary वेदस् like Sarpaveda (the science of serpents), Piśācaveda (the science of goblins), Āsuraveda (the science of demons) and Purāṇaveda (mythology).
Other topics that appear in this ब्राह्मण are: descriptions of ओङ्कार and गायत्री; details regarding the rules of ब्रह्मचर्य (which is usually spread over twelve years) needed for the study of the वेदस्; duties of the four main priests in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्; descriptions of sacrifices like अग्न्याधान, अग्निहोत्र, Darśapūrṇa-māsa, Sattra, आग्रयण, पशुबन्ध, राजसूय, वाजपेय, अश्वमेध, Sarpa-medha and others.
Gopatha is the sage who composed this work. He is one of the sages mentioned in the Atharvaveda. He probably resided in the मध्यदेश (middle part of India) and belonged to the पिप्पलाद branch of the Veda. Some of the more interesting factors mentioned here, considered as ‘new,’ are the stringent rules imposed on the ब्राह्मणस् like prohibiting them from learning मुसिच् and dancing!
Many mantras of the Ṛgveda have been quoted here.
The Uttara-Gopatha Brāhmaṇa bans receiving दक्षिणा in sacrifices.
The language of this ब्राह्मण is elegant and the definition of words appears a little peculiar.
See also BRĀHMAṆAS.

Gopāla-uttaratāpinī Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This can be considered as the latter part of the Gopāla-pūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad. There are 68 mantras, both in prose and in poetry, the two being more or less equally balanced.
The Upaniṣad starts with a parable of the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana and कृष्ण. कृष्ण advised them to give alms to the great sage दुर्वासस्. Since he lived on the opposite bank of the यमुना river, they asked कृष्ण how they could cross the river and go there. Thereupon, कृष्ण said to them to declare just once, ‘Kṛṣṇa is a ब्रह्मचारिन्, par excellence!’ and that the river would give way to them! कृष्ण also told them that whoever remembered him (with faith and devotion) would become pure and would attain the fulfilment of all desires.
The गोपीस् did as they were directed by कृष्ण and crossed the river यमुना. After meeting the sage दुर्वासस् in his hermitage and feeding him sumptuously with milk, butter and ghee and sweets prepared out of milk, they asked him how they could cross the river and get back to their homes. He advised them to remember him, ‘who had not eaten anything’ and that the river would give way!
Since these two—Kṛṣṇa being a ‘celibate’ and दुर्वासस् having ‘fasted’—were quite baffling (as proved by the यमुना river obeying their dictate), one of the गोपीस्, Gāndharvī by name, raised her doubts before the sage. The reply of the sage, interspersed with allied topics, forms the Upaniṣad proper.
Durvāsas explained that कृष्ण as the Supreme Self was beyond all the elements (like the earth, water and so on) and their products like bodies, and hence untainted by them. He was actually their inner Self.
Then, Gāndharvī asked the sage how he could know the greatness of कृष्ण who was only a cowherd boy born among them. If he were really God Himself, how was he born here, what was the मन्त्र (sacred word) by which he could be appeased and what was the mode of worship that could be offered to him.
Durvāsas replied to this question by quoting the conversation between Nārāyāṇa (Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self) and four-faced ब्रह्मा, the creator. This part of the Upaniṣad is quite long (mantras 17 to 68) and comprises several topics. They may be briefly summarised as follows:
On the top of the mountain मेरु, there are seven cities out of which मधुरा or Gopālapurī is one. But it is ब्रह्मन् Itself. This city is surrounded by twelve vanas or forests. In these vanas live the twelve Ādityas, eleven Rudras, eight वसुस्, seven Munis or sages and five Vināyakas. All these are divine and extraordinary beings.
Then comes a brief description of twelve mūrtis or forms of कृष्ण which are worshipped by the Rudras, the ṛṣis like सनक, the Vināyakas and others.
Meditation on कृष्ण, that he is our own आत्मन् or सोउल्, will ultimately lead to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. This is the next topic.
This is followed by a description of the mahimā or greatness of the city of मधुरा where the Lord कृष्ण resides. The content of the next few mantras is the fourfold form (caturvyūhas) of कृष्ण.
A detailed procedure of ध्यान or meditation on कृष्ण in one’s heart as also the symbology of the various weapons and ornaments is given in the next part.
The last part concludes the Upaniṣad with namaskāras or obeisance to कृष्ण and his various forms and manifestations in the universe.

gopura
(‘that which protects the town or city’)
------------------------------------------
A गोपुर is any high structure from where representatives of the armed forces can keep a watch over the movements of men and materials that may prove harmful to the society or the country.
Gradually, and in common parlance, it came to be associated with the towers built over the temples, both on the sanctum and on the outer walls. The former, generally small in size, are called ‘vimāna’ and the latter, usually of gigantic proportions, are termed ‘gopura’.
According to the treatises on Hindu architecture like the Mānasāra, gopuras are of ten types and can have as many as sixteen or seventeen storeys.
Gopuras are built at the main entrances of temples. In the case of big temples they can be situated in all the four directions, if a high wall is surrounding them.
Temple gopuras are generally of three types: नागर, द्राविड and वेसर. The नागर गोपुर is a curvilinear tower. The द्राविड गोपुर is in the form of a truncated pyramid. The वेसर type combines in itself both these features.
The गोपुर is generally constructed with a stone base and the superstructure of brick and mortar. It is rectangular in shape. The exterior walls are covered with sculpture of stucco.
The various storeys of the गोपुर are similar but the sizes and dimensions become gradually smaller. The top will be shaped like a semi-circular drum and is capped with kalaśas or finials which may be 3 or 5 or 7 or 9.
The gopuras of some temples in South India are noteworthy. They are those at Tiruccirapalli, चिदम्बरम्, श्रीरङ्गम्, Tañjāvūr, काञ्चीपुरम्, मदुरै, (all in Tamil Nadu) and हम्पि (in Karnataka).

Gopāla-pūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Modern scholars generally divide the Upaniṣads—the basic scriptures of Vedānta philosophy—into two groups: The Major उपनिषद्स् and the Minor उपनिषद्स्. The words ‘major’ and ‘minor’ do not refer to their size but only to the importance given to them by the earliest of the three well-known ācāryas, viz., शङ्कर (A.

-1317). The ten उपनिषद्स् upon which he has written commentaries and 3 or 4 more which he has quoted in his famous exposi-tion of the Brahmasūtras, are generally considered as ‘major’ since they may be taken as more ancient and authoritative.
The number of the minor उपनिषद्स् is considerably large. Among them one group of उपनिषद्स् goes by a common term ‘Tāpinī’. They are five in number:
Gaṇeśatāpinī Upaniṣad, Gopāla-tāpinī Upaniṣad, Nṛsiṁhatāpinī Upaniṣad, Śrīrāmatāpinī Upaniṣad and Tripurātāpinī Upaniṣad. Out of these, except the last, all the others are divided into two parts—the pūrva (former) and the uttara (latter).
The Gopāla-pūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad which is assigned to the Atharvaveda has 49 mantras divided into 6 ‘Upaniṣads’ or sections. It is in the form of a dialogue between some sages and a ब्राह्मण who was a knower of ब्रह्मन्.
The first section describes कृष्ण as the Supreme God. He is also known as Govinda (‘one who is known by the वेदस्’) and Gopījanavallabha (‘dear to the गोपीस्’ or ‘the basis of the world-appearance’ or ‘the inspirer of all sciences’). One who meditates upon him, becomes immortal.
Then comes a short description of his form (the usual कृष्ण-form) which facilitates meditation on him.
This is followed by the मन्त्र of Gopālakṛṣṇa for purposes of जप. The मन्त्र which has five words (and hence called ‘pañcapada’) is: klīm kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā. The repetition of this मन्त्र ultimately leads to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Next follow some practical instructions needed to draw the यन्त्र of Govinda along with the मन्त्र known as Anaṅga-gāyatrī (kāmadevāya vidmahe, puṣpa-bāṇāya dhīmahi, tanno’naṅgaḥ praco-dayāt) and worship of the पीठ (throne) of the Lord.
Sṛṣṭi or च्रेअतिओन् of the world has always remained a mystery. In answer to a query regarding the same, the ब्राह्मण replies that the Lord creates the world out of the eighteen letters of the मन्त्र given above (klīm kṛṣṇāya...).
This मन्त्र from which proceeded the च्रेअतिओन् of the world, is also the one that conferred Self-knowledge on महेश्वर-शिव. It is also identical with वासुदेव (Kṛṣṇa) himself.
A beautiful hymn of obeisance to Śrī कृष्ण is given next.
The Upaniṣad ends with the statement that hymning to कृष्ण and meditating upon him will result in freedom from transmigratory existence.

gopīcandana
------------------------------------------
According to the आगमस् and the पुराणस्, every Hindu is expected to wear a पुण्ड्र or a religious mark, appropriate to his cult or sect, on the forehead and also on the specified parts of the body. This पुण्ड्र may be ūrdhva (upright) or tiryak (crosswise). The nāma and the गोपीचन्दन of the Vaiṣṇavas belong to the former category and the विभूति (holy ash) to the latter.
The गोपीचन्दन is yellowish clay available near the lake called Gopītālāb, in Gujarat, in the vicinity of द्वारका, the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे. It has to be mixed with water to prepare a thin paste and then applied on the forehead, arms, shoulders and the belly. It is better to use that water with which a शालग्राम (round stone symbol of विष्णु) has been bathed. The paste has to be sanctified further by the repetition of the Gāyatrīmantra, three times.
Clay collected from such sacred places as श्रीरङ्गम् (Tamil Nadu), Siṁhācala (Andhra Pradesh), प्रयाग (Uttar Pradesh) and also from the earth near the root of तुलसी plants is also used for this purpose.

Gopāṣṭamī
(‘eighth day [connected with] Gopa [Kṛṣṇa]’)
------------------------------------------
Great men like कृष्ण have left an indelible impression upon the collective psyche of the Hindus. Even a small incident in his life becomes a great event, fit for celebration. गोपाष्टमी is one such.
Kṛṣṇa as a little boy was given the task of grazing and looking after the calves only. He was too small to take care of the cows and the bulls.
But when he grew older, into boyhood or adolescence, he had to be given the charge of cows and bulls too! The day on which this was done—it being Kārttika śukla aṣṭamī, eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika (November)—was declared as गोपाष्टमी, to be specially celebrated by feeding the cows, worshipping them and then circumambulating them. Being pleased by this, Lord कृष्ण will fulfil all our desires.

gopīs
(‘cowherdesses’)
------------------------------------------
The गोपीस् or cowherdesses of Vṛndā-vana have been well-known in Hindu mythological and devotional literature as the supreme example of madhurabhakti or bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्, loving God as one’s beloved.
Though the Mahābhārata is the earliest record of कृष्ण’s life, it does not contain accounts of his childhood and boyhood days. This has been supplied by three works: the Harivaṁśa, the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Bhāgavata. These पुराणस् give a fairly detailed account of the early life of कृष्ण, which also contain a lot of material about the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana.
Their love for कृष्ण was intense. They also knew, in their heart of hearts, that कृष्ण was not human but the Supreme Lord himself (vide Bhāgavata 10.31.3, 9). They were actually goddesses of हेअवेन् reborn on earth to play their role in the Lord’s life (ibid. 10.1.23).
Medieval schools of philosophy of the कृष्ण cults have pictured these गोपीस् as manifestations of the शक्ति or the divine power of God. If लक्ष्मी and भूदेवी represent the aiśvaryaśakti, the गोपीस् represent the mādhuryaśakti.
In the अचिन्त्य-भेदाभेद स्छोओल् of चैतन्य (A.

-1533), राधा, the chief of the गोपीस् stands for the ह्लादिनी-शक्ति of कृष्ण, the Supreme God.
See also BHĀGAVATA and KṚṢṆA.

Gopīgītā
(‘song of the गोपीस्’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgīta has created such a tremendous impression on the Hindu psyche that several religious works or authors of later years have produced their own gītās in imitation of the original Gītā. Among such gītās that find a place in the well-known Vaiṣṇava scripture, the Bhāgavata, the Kapilagītā, (3.25 to 33) and the Uddhavagītā (11.7 to 29) are more well-known.
The Gopīgītā, also called Gopikāgītā, is actually the prayer-hymn of the गोपीस् contained in the tenth skandha of this work (chapter 31). There are only 19 verses (all in the Triṣṭubh metre except one) in it.
Being attracted by the bewitching मुसिच् emanating from कृष्ण’s flute who is sitting on the bank of the river यमुना, one night, the गोपीस् of Vraja (Vṛndāvana) rush to him. As if taken by surprise, he non-chalantly advises them to return home. Since they are deeply in love with him, they refuse. Then कृष्ण sports with them for some time. This rouses their pride and superiority-complex. So, he suddenly disappears from their midst. Smitten with anguish and even indignation, they madly search for him, weeping and wailing piteously. Not finding him anywhere they assemble together on the sandy bank and start singing prayers to him. It is this prayer of theirs that forms the Gopīgītā (Bhāgavata 10.3

).
These nineteen verses are highly poetic and full of pathos, often reflecting erotic sentiments. Though they were panting for reunion with him, they were also fully conscious of his being the Supreme Lord of the universe and the inner Self of all of them (vide verses 4, 9 and 18).
As regards the propriety of कृष्ण’s amorous play with them, शुक gives a detailed explanation, in reply to the questions raised by the king परीक्षित् himself (vide 10.33.27-40).
The love of the गोपीस् towards Lord कृष्ण has been categorised as ‘madhura-भाव’ or ‘bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्’ which has been recognised by Christianity and Sufism also.
